procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated May 24, 1967 of the Assam and Nagaland High Court in Civil Rule No. 425 of 1966, dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellant.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a writ petition on November 3, 1966. Justice Dutta, acting as a Vacation Judge, entertained the petition at Sibsagar and passed interim orders. A preliminary objection was raised in the High Court regarding the maintainability of the petition, arguing that Justice Dutta could not act as a Judge while working as a Commission of Enquiry and lacked jurisdiction at Sibsagar. The High Court dismissed the petition on May 24, 1967, holding that the original presentation was irregular.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's dismissal of the writ petition. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and sent the case back to the High Court. The Supreme Court directed the High Court to reconsider whether the petition should be admitted, treating it as represented when it reached Gauhati, and if so, to set it down for hearing.

directions: Set aside the order of the High Court dismissing the writ petition.

Send it back to the High Court with the direction that the High Court should reconsider whether the petition should be admitted, taking it as represented on the day it reached Gauhati, and if so it should be set down for hearing in due course.

issue.issue_text: Whether a High Court Judge, while appointed to a Commission of Enquiry, can still act as a Judge of the High Court.

facts: A Judge of the High Court (Dutta J.) was appointed to head a Commission of Enquiry.
At the same time, he was also nominated to be the Vacation Judge for the High Court.
The Chief Justice of the High Court held that the Judge could not perform the duties of a High Court Judge while also working on the Commission.
law: When a High Court Judge is appointed to a Commission of Enquiry, they do not give up ('demit') their office as a Judge.
Such appointments to Commissions are typically temporary, and their sittings are not continuous.
An appointment to a Commission of Enquiry does not deprive the Judge of the rights and privileges of their judicial office.
A distinction is made between a temporary, non-continuous commission and a whole-time post. If a judge is appointed to a whole-time post, they cannot simultaneously work as a High Court Judge.
application: The Supreme Court noted that it is common for High Court Judges to be appointed to head temporary Commissions of Enquiry.
Because these commissions are not whole-time posts and do not sit continuously, the Judge remains a part of the High Court.
Therefore, the Judge is entitled to sit and act as a Judge of the High Court in the intervals when the Commission is not sitting or whenever they have time to do so.
The Court found that the Judge's appointment as a Vacation Judge while heading the Commission was 'quite in order'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a High Court Judge appointed to a temporary Commission of Enquiry can still act as a Judge of the High Court. The Court reasoned that such an appointment is not a whole-time post, and the Judge does not give up their judicial office. Consequently, they are entitled to perform their judicial duties whenever the Commission is not sitting.

issue.issue_text: Whether a writ petition should be dismissed merely on the ground that its original presentation to a judge was irregular (i.e., at a place other than the seat of the High Court).

facts: A writ petition was urgently presented to a Vacation Judge at Sibsagar, even though the official seat of the High Court was at Gauhati.
The judge entertained the petition and passed an interim order at Sibsagar.
Subsequently, the papers related to the writ petition were sent to the High Court at Gauhati and were dealt with there.
The High Court later dismissed the petition, reasoning that the initial presentation at Sibsagar was irregular and improper.
law: A procedural irregularity, such as presenting a petition at a location other than the official seat of the court, does not automatically invalidate the petition itself.
Such an irregularity can be cured if the petition subsequently reaches the proper court and is dealt with there.
application: The Supreme Court assumed, for the sake of argument, that the presentation of the petition at Sibsagar was irregular.
However, the Court found that this initial irregularity was cured when the petition was later sent to the High Court's seat at Gauhati and was handled by the court there.
The Court held that the petition should be considered as having been "re-presented" to the High Court on the date it reached Gauhati.
While the interim order passed at Sibsagar might also have been irregular, this did not justify dismissing the entire petition once the procedural defect was corrected.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was wrong to dismiss the writ petition merely on the ground that its original presentation was irregular. The irregularity was cured when the petition reached the High Court's proper seat, and therefore, the High Court should have proceeded to consider the petition on its merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the remarks made by the Chief Justice against a colleague, suggesting "unholy haste and hurry", were justified in the circumstances.

facts: An appellant, needing to sit for an examination starting on November 4th, learned on November 2nd that he would not be allowed to.
As it was a court vacation, the appellant presented an urgent petition to the only available judge, the Vacation Judge (Dutta J.), who was at Sibsagar, not the High Court's main seat.
Dutta J. entertained the petition on November 3rd and passed an order allowing the appellant to take the exam.
The case was later heard by a bench including the Chief Justice, who set aside Dutta J.'s order.
In his judgment, the Chief Justice made critical remarks, stating that Dutta J. had exhibited "unholy haste and hurry" and an "unnecessary zeal... to assist the appellant".
law: Judicial decorum must be maintained at all times.
Even when there is justification for criticizing another judge, the language used must be dignified and of utmost restraint.
application: The Supreme Court analyzed the circumstances and found that the appellant faced an urgent situation with the examination imminent.
The Court determined that the steps taken by the Vacation Judge (Dutta J.) were the "only steps that could have been taken" in the situation.

The Court reasoned that once Dutta J. decided he had jurisdiction, his subsequent actions to ensure the order was effective before the exam were proper and could not be characterized as "unholy haste and hurry" or "unnecessary zeal".
The Court found there was "no justification at all" for the Chief Justice's remarks and that they were made "without any basis".
It was noted that such remarks are uncalled for even against subordinate court judges with clear evidence of impropriety, and are even more objectionable when made against a colleague.
The Court concluded that the Chief Justice's remarks were "entirely uncalled for", made a "sorry reading", and brought the High Court into disrepute.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the Chief Justice's remarks, holding that they were entirely unjustified and uncalled for in the circumstances. The Court found that the Vacation Judge's actions were appropriate given the urgency of the matter and that the Chief Justice's criticism lacked any basis and violated the principles of judicial decorum.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a writ petition should be dismissed merely on the ground that its original presentation to a judge was irregular (i.e., at a place other than the seat of the High Court).
appellant_arguments: The petition should not have been dismissed simply because its initial presentation was irregular.
The petition should have been considered as properly presented when it reached the High Court's seat at Gauhati and should have been dealt with on its merits.
respondent_arguments: The irregular presentation of the petition was a valid ground for its dismissal (as held by one of the High Court judges).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the remarks made by the Chief Justice against a colleague, suggesting "unholy haste and hurry", were justified in the circumstances.
appellant_arguments: The remarks were "entirely uncalled for" and unjustified.
The urgency of the situation (the appellant learned on Nov 2 that he could not sit for an exam starting Nov 4) justified the judge's swift action.
respondent_arguments: The remarks were justified as the judge exhibited "unholy haste and hurry" and showed "an unnecessary zeal on his part to assist the appellant".

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An irregularity in the presentation of a petition is cured when the petition subsequently comes before the High Court, and the petition should not be dismissed solely on the ground of that initial irregularity.
obiter: Judicial decorum must be maintained at all times.
Even where criticism of another judge is justified, it must be expressed in language of utmost restraint and dignity.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court erred in dismissing the writ petition on the procedural ground of its initial irregular presentation, as that irregularity was cured once the petition reached the seat of the High Court. Furthermore, the High Court Chief Justice's remarks against his colleague, suggesting "unholy haste and hurry," were entirely uncalled for and without justification. Given the judge's belief that he had jurisdiction and the urgency of the matter, his swift actions were the only proper steps to take and did not reflect improper zeal.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the principle that a procedural irregularity in the presentation of a petition is cured when the petition subsequently reaches the proper venue (the seat of the High Court), at which point it should be considered as properly represented and dealt with on its merits.
policy_considerations: Judicial decorum must be maintained at all times.
Criticism of a judicial colleague in a judgment is highly objectionable, especially when made without any justification or basis.
Even where criticism of another judge is justified, it must be expressed in language of utmost restraint and dignity.
Making unjustified critical remarks against a colleague brings the High Court into disrepute.
